fetched_contents.text: Two Pathways for the Degradation of Orpiment Pigment (As2S3) Found in Paintings Abstract Paintings are complex objects containing many different chemical compounds that can react over time. The degradation of arsenic sulfide pigments causes optical changes in paintings. The main degradation product was thought to be white arsenolite (As2O3), but previous research also showed the abundant presence of As(V) species. In this study, we investigate the influence of the presence of a medium on the degradation mechanism of orpiment (As2S3) using synchrotron radiation (SR)-based tomographic transmission X-ray microscopy, SR-based micro-X-ray fluorescence, and X-ray absorption near edge structure spectroscopy. Upon direct illumination of dry orpiment powder using UV–visible light, only the formation of As2O3 was observed. When As2S3 was surrounded by a medium and illuminated, As2O3 was only observed in the area directly exposed to light, while As(V) degradation species were found elsewhere in the medium. Without accelerated artificial light aging, As(V)(aq) species are formed and migrate throughout the medium within weeks after preparation. In both scenarios, the As(V) species form via intermediate As(III)(aq) species and the presence of a medium is necessary. As(V)(aq) species can react with available cations to form insoluble metal arsenates, which induces stress within the paint layers (leading to, e.g., cracks and delamination) or can lead to a visual change of the image of the painting. Introduction Works of art painted with arsenic sulfide pigments are known to be affected by degradation phenomena.1−7 These degradation phenomena can manifest themselves in different ways. Optical changes in the paint can be caused by a color loss of the arsenic sulfide pigment and the formation of new chemical species. The degradation can also result in structural changes of the paint such as flaking or chalking. All of these degradation forms can cause aesthetic damage to the works of art. This work focusses on arsenic sulfide degradation in oil paintings. An example of an oil painting affected by the degradation of arsenic sulfide is “Still Life with Flowers in a Glass Vase” (1650–1683) by Jan Davidszoon de Heem (Figure 1, middle). The yellow eglantine rose in the middle of the painting today looks flat and without many features. This is a result of a change in optical effects due to the degradation of the arsenic sulfides that were originally present.8 Such changes often result in a loss of depth and of details created by the artist. In this work, the degradation phenomena were studied by investigating the pigment powder, model systems containing the pigment and a relevant paint sample of the painting by De Heem. Figure 1 shows an overview of the work performed in this study. Artists have been aware of problems associated with arsenic sulfide pigments for a long time. In the medieval text “Mappae Clavicula” (12th century), the incompatibility of arsenic sulfide pigments with some other pigments containing copper and lead was already described.9 It is also mentioned in artist manuals such as “De groote waereld in ’t klein geschildert” by Wilhelmus Beurs and “Il Libro Dell’Arte” by Cennino Cennini.10,11 However, these archival works only describe reactions that take place on a short time scale and their authors were seemingly not aware of degradation phenomena related to arsenic sulfide observed on longer time scales. The two main arsenic sulfide pigments are realgar and orpiment. Realgar (As4S4) is an orange to red pigment, while orpiment (As2S3) is yellow. Next to these crystalline materials, there exist non-stoichiometric, glassy phases with the general formula AsxSy.12−15 The oxidation state of As is +3 or lower in all these compounds. The earliest documented use of these pigments dates back to ancient Egypt (16th to 11th century B.C.)16 and was continued until the end of the 19th century. The high toxicity and their incompatibility with some other pigments were two of the reasons for the decline in popularity of arsenic sulfide pigments.17 The degradation of realgar (As4S4) is described in literature as a photo-induced process taking place upon illumination with visible light; the degradation pathway has been extensively studied. Realgar is thought to undergo a transformation through an intermediate χ-phase (As4S5), resulting in the formation of a combination of para-realgar (As4S4) and arsenolite (As2O3, with As in the +3 oxidation state).1,12,18−21 The exact degradation pathway of orpiment has been investigated less intensively. Studies have shown that light exposure results in the direct formation of arsenolite (As2O3). Vermeulen et al. proposed the breaking of the arsenic–sulfur bond and the release of sulfur as H2S in this degradation mechanism.3 However, for both realgar as well as orpiment, arsenolite is not the only arsenic-based degradation product. Recent studies on paint cross sections have shown that the presence of arsenic species is not constrained to the paint layer originally containing the arsenic sulfide pigment.2,4,5 These X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) studies showed that arsenic species with a +5 oxidation state were found in paint layers above and below the original arsenic sulfide paint layer as well as in the varnish layers and, in the case of a painting on a wooden support in the wood structure. These As(V) species derive from the arsenic sulfide pigment and are very mobile. They are therefore able to migrate through all the different paint layers. By using a combination of macro and micro X-ray diffraction (μ-XRD), Simoen et al. have shown that the mobile As(V) species, in the presence of Pb2+ ions, can form new, secondary degradation products, such as the lead arsenate minerals mimetite and schultenite.6,22 In this study, we took a closer look at the formation of mobile As(V) species in orpiment powder and orpiment containing paints. fetched_contents.text: Pigment analysis by Raman microscopy and portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) of thirteenth to fourteenth century illuminations and cuttings from Bologna Abstract Non-destructive pigment analysis by Raman microscopy (RM) and portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) has been carried out on some Bolognese illuminations and cuttings chosen to represent the beginnings, evolution and height of Bolognese illuminated manuscript production. Dating to the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries and held in a private collection, the study provides evidence for the pigments generally used in this period. The results, which are compared with those obtained for other north Italian artwork, show the developments in usage of artistic materials and technique. Also addressed in this study is an examination of the respective roles of RM and pXRF analysis in this area of technical art history. This article is part of the themed issue ‘Raman spectroscopy in art and archaeology’. Keywords: Raman microscopy, pigments, portable X-ray fluorescence, illuminated manuscripts and cuttings, Bologna 1. Introduction Technical art history studies of illuminated manuscripts and cuttings ranging in date from the Anglo-Saxon period (eighth century) to late medieval times are numerous. This situation owes much to the role of Raman microscopy (RM) which has been notably successful in achieving high-resolution identifications of pigments. As a result, the evolution of developments in artistic materials from the Roman period onwards is becoming better understood. The Roman palette used in wall paintings was dominated by locally available minerals, earths and plant extracts with a limited range of synthetic materials such as lead white, verdigris, red lead and Egyptian blue [1–3]. It was later supplemented by other pigments as painting media and techniques diversified in the Byzantine and neighbouring worlds. One such pigment was lazurite (extracted from lapis lazuli found in Afghanistan) which was identified as a blue pigment in the earliest (i.e. tenth to thirteenth century) Armenian and Byzantine manuscripts reviewed by Orna [4]. By the fourteenth century, if not earlier, communications by land or sea had enabled painters working in many parts of Europe to access a wide variety of pigments. Besides technical treatises, expertise was probably passed on orally and through practical experience [5]. But underlying the basic commonality of the palette at that time was the way that individual artists could improvise or experiment, according to the status or scale of the manuscript, by mixing colours that were already part of that palette. One of the issues considered in this paper is the variability in artistic materials achieved through improvisation or experiment at the local, intra-school level and within a well-defined period. In the earlier ‘Middle Ages’, most books were produced in monasteries and other major church establishments [6]. The first RM study of an Anglo-Saxon manuscript was made on the Lindisfarne Gospels, which revealed (contrary to perceived wisdom of the day) no trace of lazurite on the manuscript; the blue colour was achieved solely by the use of indigo extracted from the woad plant indigenous in northeast England and Scotland [7]. By contrast and dating a century later (ca AD 800), the painters of the Book of Kells in Ireland made the same use of indigo but also employed lazurite [8]. Differential access to lazurite was surely an issue at the time as this pigment was not found on any of the other eighth, ninth and tenth century manuscripts studied in the British Library [9] until it was identified as a ca AD 920 pigmentary addition made as part of the restoration of a much earlier manuscript [10]. With the growth of cities and the evolution of the ‘Gothic’ styles from the ‘Romanesque’ between 1100 and 1200, professional resident bookmakers and mendicant clergy took over from monks. Notable sites were the universities of Paris and Bologna, and later university cities. One of the earliest manuscript studies by RM was of a thirteenth century Paris bible, in which the following pigments were identified: azurite, orpiment, lazurite, realgar, lead white, red lead, malachite and vermilion [11]. A second early study was of the Skard manuscript, a finely illuminated fourteenth century Icelandic manuscript (ca 1360). The pigments identified were vermilion, orpiment, realgar, red ochre, azurite, bone white, verdigris and possibly green earth [12]. Notable was the absence of lead-containing pigments, but whether this was due to stylistic preferences or non-availability of lead pigments in Iceland is not known. We report here the results of a programme of non-destructive analysis of five illuminations and cuttings of the Bologna school in northern Italy using RM and portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF). They were chosen to represent the beginnings, evolution and height of Bolognese illuminated manuscript production from examples in a private collection readily available for such analysis; they date to the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries and provide at least a partial indication of the pigments generally used in this period, though those used in many legal and other academic manuscripts are under-represented, as are the finest pigments of the most luxurious Bolognese productions from the Palaeologan Renaissance ‘Second Style’. fetched_contents.text: Analytical imaging studies of the migration of degraded orpiment, realgar, and emerald green pigments in historic paintings and related conservation issues Background Yellow orpiment (As2S3) and red–orange realgar (As4S4), used by artists from different cultures since antiquity, and emerald green (Cu(C2H3O2)2·3Cu(AsO2)2), a popular brilliant green pigment first synthesized by Willem Sattler in 1814, are pigments that contain arsenic. They have all been found to be unstable in paints. Photo-degradation of realgar (As4S4) and orpiment (As2S3) results in sensitive, transparent, whitish, friable and/or crumbling paints, while chemically degraded emerald green pigment (Cu(C2H3O2)2·3Cu(AsO2)2, copper (II) acetoarsenite) in oil paint leads to transparent, dark brown layers [1] or stains on paper [2]. The degradation of these arsenic-containing pigments seriously affects the appearance and stability of paintings and painted objects, the chemical changes are irreversible, and the accompanying physical changes to the rest of the object worsen the conservation problems. The physical alteration associated with the chemical degradation, often seen as cracking and crumbling of paint layers and surfaces, further enhances the degradation and poses a major conservation challenge [3, 4]. The cracked surfaces easily collect dirt from the environment, accentuating the discolored regions, and are vulnerable to further degradation when exposed to moisture and solvents during treatment. While discolored and crumbling paint can be consolidated, it cannot be readily cleaned. The open, porous structure creates an unvarnished painting (or painted furniture)-like surface. Re-varnishing the affected regions of the work, unfortunately, does not mitigate the problem because the highly mobile degradation products migrate through the varnish. The previous study indicated that the photo-degradation products of orpiment and realgar are highly water soluble, and consequently they do not remain at the location of the original pigment in the paint, but migrate throughout the whole multi-layered paint system [5]. For example, the investigation of an early eighteenth-century chest on stand that had been repeatedly varnished after the application of an orpiment design showed that the photo-oxidized arsenic species had migrated through each varnish layer, with larger deposits visible at the interface of each pair of layers [5]. Migrated and dispersed products containing arsenic also form a potential health hazard during conservation practice. The conservator might not be aware that arsenic is likely to be present in, and at the surface of, varnish layers further away from the degraded arsenic-containing paint layers. In the case of paintings, conservation practice often involves the removal and replacement of discolored varnishes. In addition, when original pigment material has migrated into these varnishes, and their removal will expose friable altered paint while not improving the color of the altered pigment underneath, it may actually be prudent to consider leaving the varnish intact in these discolored regions. In the case of painted American furniture, conservation practice typically consists of leaving the full finish history of the object intact, unless the figure of the wood or the painted decoration is completely obscured. In this case the topmost layers of finish will be mechanically reduced by careful sanding, which again leads to a health hazard with arsenic species having migrated into these uppermost varnish layers. Like many photo-oxidation problems observed in artists’ pigments, often the original brightly colored paint can be observed below the discolored and flaking altered paint. This has led to the undesirable consequence of folk/vernacular art objects exhibiting this type of alteration to be “skinned” by untrained restorers, removing the artists’ original but damaged material to reveal the bright colors underneath. While such a restoration presents the owner or potential buyer with an attractive presentation surface, not only has original artist’s material been removed, but the pigments thus exposed lose the protection of the overlying alteration crust and will most likely experience rapid degradation. The degradation of realgar and orpiment is triggered by light within the wavelength range of 500–670 nm. The highest degradation efficiency is in the green part of the visible light spectrum (530–560 nm) [6]. In the first step of light induced degradation, realgar undergoes polymorphism and becomes friable and bright yellow, (AsxSy, para-realgar) and subsequently degrades further to a white phase (As2O3, arsenolite). The photo-oxidation of orpiment, on the other hand, results directly in a white product (arsenolite), often appearing as a dirty/off white color or an ocherous material because of the presence of an overlying varnish [6, 7]. In objects painted with large fields of orpiment, the degradation is often not uniform, resulting in a mix of ivory to ochre yellow [8]. The degradation products of arsenic sulfide pigments have been observed and identified in painted works of art by visual observation, µRaman spectroscopy, and X-ray diffraction [9–18]. One limitation of using µRaman spectroscopy to study realgar is the danger of creating para-realgar during the analysis due to the pigment’s extreme photo-sensitivity. So far, para-realgar and arsenic trioxide have been consistently identified as the main oxidation products of arsenic sulfide pigments. Recent synchrotron radiation-based arsenic (As) K–edge micro X-ray absorption near edge structure (μ-XANES) studies following preliminary µFTIR studies revealed another set of degradation products, i.e. arsenate compounds (As5+) present as calcium, lead, aluminum and iron arsenates depending on the pigments and fillers surrounding the original arsenic sulfide pigments [5]. Mini-report on the chemistry and synthesis of orpiment and realgar

Orpiment and realgar are both arsenic sulfide pigments, but they differ in their exact chemical formulas and structural properties. Orpiment has the formula As₂S₃ [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R5], while realgar has the formula α-As₄S₄ [N1-R1][N1-R4]. These are the primary stoichiometric forms described in the evidence; however, the evidence also notes that both pigments exist in non-stoichiometric, glassy phases with general formula AsxSy [N2-F1], which is important for understanding historical variability.

Historically, both pigments were formed and purified from arsenic sulfide minerals. Orpiment is a monoclinic arsenic sulfide mineral with a Mohs hardness of 1.5 to 2 and a specific gravity of 3.49 [N1-R3]. Realgar is similarly a soft arsenic sulfide mineral, with a Mohs hardness of 1.5–2.0 and a density of 3.56–3.59 g/ml [N1-R1][N1-R4]. The evidence also indicates that these materials have been used since antiquity, with realgar described as “arsenic blende, ruby sulphur or ruby of arsenic” and orpiment as a yellow to yellow-orange pigment [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The historical context in N5 reinforces that these pigments were used by artists across cultures and periods, including in paintings and manuscripts [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5][N5-F4].

Crystallinity, particle size, and color stability are key differences between the two pigments. Realgar is described as an orange to red pigment [N2-F1], while orpiment is yellow [N2-F1]. The evidence also notes that realgar can undergo polymorphism under light, becoming friable and bright yellow (para-realgar) and then further degrading to a white phase (arsenolite) [N5-F4]. Orpiment, by contrast, tends to form arsenolite directly under light [N5-F4][N2-F1]. The evidence further indicates that both pigments can exist in non-stoichiometric, glassy phases [N2-F1], which may affect particle size and crystallinity in historical samples. The N5 evidence also emphasizes that these pigments degrade irreversibly and can migrate through paint layers after light-induced damage [N5-F4], which is a structural and color-stability issue that matters for conservation.

In summary, orpiment and realgar are chemically distinct arsenic sulfide pigments with different formulas and color behavior, while both are historically formed as soft, low-hardness minerals and can exhibit structural variability. Orpiment is yellow, realgar is orange-red, and both can degrade under light into arsenolite and other byproducts, making their color and structural stability very sensitive to environmental exposure [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N2-F1][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N9:
Mini-report on degradation mechanisms and products

The degradation of orpiment and realgar is primarily driven by light, especially visible light in the 500–670 nm range, with the highest degradation efficiency in the green part of the visible spectrum (530–560 nm) [N4-F3][N5-F4]. Light-induced degradation is the main mechanism described in the evidence, and it is linked to the formation of toxic or unstable byproducts. Realgar undergoes a photo-induced transformation through an intermediate χ-phase (As₄S₅), resulting in para-realgar and arsenolite (As₂O₃) [N2-F1]. Orpiment also degrades under light, producing arsenolite directly [N5-F4][N2-F1]. The evidence explicitly notes that arsenolite is a white arsenic trioxide product and that arsenate compounds (As⁵⁺) can also form [N5-F4]. These byproducts are not only chemically unstable but also highly mobile, capable of migrating through paint layers and varnish [N5-F4].

Humidity and temperature also play a role in the degradation of arsenic sulfide pigments. The evidence in N4 states that light and humidity are key factors in the degradation of arsenic-containing pigments, and that high temperatures accelerate chemical reactions driving up the rate of overall degradation [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3]. While the direct evidence for humidity-induced degradation of orpiment and realgar is less explicit than for light, the broader conservation context clearly links environmental conditions to accelerated deterioration [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that the degradation of realgar and orpiment is triggered by light, and that the highest degradation efficiency is in visible light [N4-F3][N5-F4]. Together, these factors indicate that the degradation of both pigments is a multi-stimulus process, with light being the primary trigger and humidity/temperature acting as accelerants.

Degradation affects both color and structural integrity. Light-induced degradation causes realgar to become friable and bright yellow before progressing to a white phase, while orpiment tends to form a white arsenolite product [N5-F4]. The evidence also states that the degradation products can migrate through the entire multi-layered paint system [N5-F4], which compromises structural integrity by creating cracks, delamination, and a porous surface [N5-F4]. In addition, the physical alteration associated with chemical degradation worsens conservation problems by increasing exposure to dirt and moisture [N5-F4]. The result is irreversible damage, loss of detail and depth, and a more vulnerable object that is harder to conserve [N5-F4].

In terms of toxic byproducts, the evidence is explicit: arsenolite and arsenate compounds are formed, and arsenates can spread throughout the paint layers [N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that the presence of a medium can influence the degradation pathway, with As(V) species forming and migrating in the presence of a medium [N2-F1]. This means that historical artworks containing these pigments may have dangerous arsenic species present in unexpected locations, including varnish layers and the support structure [N5-F4]. Overall, the degradation mechanisms of orpiment and realgar are light-dominated, with humidity and temperature accelerating damage, and the byproducts are toxic, unstable, and structurally destructive [N2-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N10:
Mini-report on analytical detection and conservation relevance

Several analytical techniques are used to distinguish orpiment and realgar in artworks. The evidence strongly supports Raman microscopy and X-ray fluorescence (XRF) as the main methods. A study of thirteenth- to fourteenth-century illuminations and cuttings used Raman microscopy and portable XRF, and identified realgar, orpiment, and other pigments [N3-F2]. Another study combined MA-XRF, p-XRD, p-Raman, and cross-section analysis to discover artificial orpiment in a historical painting [N3-R2]. The evidence also notes that Raman microscopy is considered the best single technique for pigment identification and is especially effective when used with other methods [N3-R4]. XRF is similarly highlighted as a portable and non-destructive method used alongside Raman [N3-R1][N3-F2]. In addition, the evidence indicates that µRaman spectroscopy has been used to study realgar and related degraded compounds [N5-F4], while X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) have been used to identify arsenic sulfide degradation products [N5-F4].

False positives and cross-reactivity are an important issue. The evidence notes that µRaman spectroscopy can be problematic for realgar because the pigment is extremely photosensitive, and para-realgar can form during analysis [N5-F4]. This means that even the analytical process itself can alter the sample and produce misleading results. The evidence also mentions that arsenic sulfide pigments can be confused with other materials because their degradation products may appear in unexpected places, including varnish layers and the support structure [N5-F4]. This cross-reactivity is especially important in conservation because it affects how conservators interpret analytical results and how they treat the object [N5-F4].

Conservation choices depend heavily on analysis because the presence of arsenic sulfide pigments has major implications for handling and treatment. The evidence states that the degradation products are highly mobile and can migrate through paint layers, varnish, and even into the support structure [N5-F4]. This means that conservation interventions such as varnish removal, sanding, or cleaning can expose friable altered paint and may actually worsen the problem by removing protective layers [N5-F4]. The evidence also warns that re-varnishing does not mitigate the problem because the mobile degradation products migrate through the varnish [N5-F4]. Therefore, analytical detection informs whether a pigment is present, how it has degraded, and what risks are associated with conservation actions [N3-F2][N5-F4]. In short, the combination of Raman and XRF is the most relevant analytical framework for distinguishing orpiment and realgar, but cross-reactivity and the photosensitivity of realgar mean interpretation must be cautious [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-F2][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N11:
Mini-report on environmental handling and preservation strategies

The best storage and display conditions for both orpiment and realgar are low light, controlled temperature, and controlled humidity. The evidence directly links light, humidity, and temperature to degradation, with light being the main trigger and humidity/temperature acting as accelerants [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-F3]. Specifically, the evidence states that the degradation of realgar and orpiment is triggered by light in the 500–670 nm range, with the highest degradation efficiency in visible light [N4-F3][N5-F4]. It also notes that high temperatures accelerate chemical reactions and overall degradation [N4-R3]. For humidity, the broader conservation context emphasizes that collections environments should monitor temperature, relative humidity, dew point, visible and UV light, and pollutants [N4-R2]. While the evidence does not provide a single recommended RH range for orpiment and realgar specifically, it clearly supports keeping relative humidity low enough to slow moisture-driven chemical reactions and avoid promoting the formation of unstable arsenic compounds [N4-R2][N4-R3].

Common conservation interventions include varnish removal, mechanical reduction of uppermost layers, and cleaning. However, the evidence warns that these interventions carry significant risks. When discolored varnishes are removed, friable altered paint can be exposed, and the altered pigment underneath may not improve in color [N5-F4]. Mechanical reduction of uppermost layers is also described as a practice used for painted furniture, but it can expose arsenic-containing species that have migrated into those layers [N5-F4]. The evidence further states that discolored and crumbling paint can be consolidated, but it cannot be readily cleaned [N5-F4]. This means that conservation choices often favor stabilization over removal when the original material is damaged and the altered layer is not easily reversible [N5-F4].

Handling affects long-term stability because arsenic-containing pigments are toxic and can release hazardous species during conservation. The evidence explicitly states that the degradation products are highly mobile and can migrate through the entire multi-layered paint system [N5-F4]. It also notes that arsenic species can collect dirt from the environment and become vulnerable to further degradation when exposed to moisture and solvents during treatment [N5-F4]. In addition, the evidence warns that conservators may not be aware that arsenic can be present in varnish layers far from the original pigment layer [N5-F4]. This handling risk is compounded by the fact that the degradation products are toxic and mobile, making them a health hazard during conservation practice [N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that orpiment can be toxic and should be handled with care [N7-R2], reinforcing that conservation handling should be protective and minimally invasive.

In summary, the best preservation strategy is to keep orpiment and realgar in dark, low-humidity, low-temperature environments and to avoid unnecessary handling and removal [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-F3]. Common interventions such as varnish removal and mechanical sanding can expose fragile altered paint and worsen the problem, so they should be used only when absolutely necessary [N5-F4]. Handling is especially risky because arsenic-containing pigments can release toxic species and migrate during treatment, making conservation choices highly dependent on analytical results and a conservative approach [N5-F4][N7-R2].

## 1) Chemical identity and historical formation

Orpiment and realgar are both arsenic sulfide pigments, but they differ chemically and structurally. Orpiment has the formula As₂S₃ [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R5], while realgar has the formula α-As₄S₄ [N1-R1][N1-R4]. Orpiment is a monoclinic arsenic sulfide mineral with a Mohs hardness of 1.5 to 2 and a specific gravity of 3.49 [N1-R3], while realgar is similarly a soft arsenic sulfide mineral with a Mohs hardness of 1.5–2.0 and a density of 3.56–3.59 g/ml [N1-R1][N1-R4]. The evidence also notes that both pigments have been used since antiquity and were commonly used in paintings and manuscripts by artists across cultures and periods [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5][N5-F4].

Crystallinity, particle size, and color stability are key differences between the two pigments. Realgar is described as an orange to red pigment [N2-F1], while orpiment is yellow [N2-F1]. The evidence also indicates that realgar can undergo polymorphism under light, becoming friable and bright yellow (para-realgar) and then further degrading to a white phase (arsenolite) [N5-F4]. Orpiment, by contrast, tends to form arsenolite directly under light [N5-F4][N2-F1]. The presence of non-stoichiometric, glassy phases in both pigments suggests that their historical samples may vary in crystallinity and particle size [N2-F1]. This structural variability is important because it can affect how the pigments behave during degradation and conservation.

## 2) Stability differences

The two pigments are both unstable in historical artworks, but their degradation behavior differs in important ways. The evidence shows that both pigments are highly sensitive to light, especially visible light in the 500–670 nm range, with the highest degradation efficiency in the green part of the visible spectrum (530–560 nm) [N4-F3][N5-F4]. However, realgar has a more complex light-induced degradation pathway than orpiment. Realgar undergoes a photo-induced transformation through an intermediate χ-phase (As₄S₅), resulting in para-realgar and arsenolite (As₂O₃) [N2-F1]. Orpiment, by contrast, tends to form arsenolite directly under light [N5-F4][N2-F1]. This means that realgar’s degradation is more stepwise and structurally complex, while orpiment’s degradation appears to be more direct.

Both pigments are also affected by environmental factors beyond light. The evidence links humidity and temperature to accelerated chemical reactions and overall degradation [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3]. High temperatures accelerate chemical reactions, while humidity is identified as a key factor in the degradation of arsenic-containing pigments [N4-R1][N4-R2]. Although the evidence is more explicit about light than about humidity and temperature alone, it clearly supports the view that these pigments are highly sensitive to environmental conditions and that stability is not guaranteed even in stable-looking objects [N4-F3][N5-F4].

## 3) Degradation mechanisms and products

The degradation of orpiment and realgar is primarily driven by light-induced oxidation. Light causes realgar to transform into para-realgar and then into arsenolite, while orpiment forms arsenolite more directly [N2-F1][N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that arsenate compounds (As⁵⁺) can form as additional degradation products [N5-F4]. These byproducts are toxic, unstable, and highly mobile. The evidence states that arsenic sulfide degradation products can migrate through the entire multi-layered paint system, including into varnish layers and even into the support structure [N5-F4]. This migration is a major conservation problem because it spreads the damage and makes the pigment’s original location difficult to identify [N5-F4].

The evidence further explains that the presence of a medium can influence the degradation pathway. In the presence of a medium, As(V) species can form and migrate throughout the medium, while As(V) species can also react with available cations to form insoluble metal arsenates [N2-F1]. This means that the degradation process is not only chemical but also structural: the formation of arsenates induces stress within paint layers and can lead to cracks and delamination [N2-F1]. The physical alteration associated with chemical degradation worsens conservation problems by increasing exposure to dirt, moisture, and solvents during treatment [N5-F4].

## 4) Effects on color and structural integrity

Degradation has a major impact on both color and structural integrity. Light-induced degradation causes realgar to become friable and bright yellow before progressing to a white phase, while orpiment tends to form a white arsenolite product [N5-F4]. The evidence also states that the degradation products can migrate through paint layers and varnish, creating a porous surface and making the object more vulnerable to further damage [N5-F4]. In addition, the physical alteration associated with chemical degradation can lead to cracking and crumbling of paint layers and surfaces, which further enhances degradation and worsens conservation problems [N5-F4]. The result is irreversible damage, loss of detail and depth, and a more fragile object that is harder to conserve [N5-F4].

The evidence also describes how degradation affects the appearance of paintings. For example, the color of the original pigment can be obscured by discolored and flaking altered paint, while the underlying original material may remain visible beneath the degradation crust [N5-F4]. This means that conservation interventions can expose the original paint but may not restore the original color. In some cases, conservation practice may actually be prudent to leave the varnish intact in discolored regions because removing it can expose friable altered paint while not improving the color underneath [N5-F4]. Overall, degradation damages both the color and the physical structure of artworks, making the pigments highly unstable in historical contexts [N5-F4][N2-F1].

## 5) Analytical detection and conservation relevance

Several analytical techniques are used to distinguish orpiment and realgar in artworks. The evidence strongly supports Raman microscopy and X-ray fluorescence (XRF) as the main methods. A study of thirteenth- to fourteenth-century illuminations and cuttings used Raman microscopy and portable XRF, and identified realgar, orpiment, and other pigments [N3-F2]. Another study combined MA-XRF, p-XRD, p-Raman, and cross-section analysis to discover artificial orpiment in a historical painting [N3-R2]. The evidence also notes that Raman microscopy is considered the best single technique for pigment identification and is especially effective when used with other methods [N3-R4]. XRF is similarly highlighted as a portable and non-destructive method used alongside Raman [N3-R1][N3-F2]. In addition, the evidence indicates that µRaman spectroscopy has been used to study realgar and related degraded compounds [N5-F4], while X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) have been used to identify arsenic sulfide degradation products [N5-F4].

False positives and cross-reactivity are an important issue. The evidence notes that µRaman spectroscopy can be problematic for realgar because the pigment is extremely photosensitive, and para-realgar can form during analysis [N5-F4]. This means that even the analytical process itself can alter the sample and produce misleading results. The evidence also mentions that arsenic sulfide pigments can be confused with other materials because their degradation products may appear in unexpected places, including varnish layers and the support structure [N5-F4]. This cross-reactivity is especially important in conservation because it affects how conservators interpret analytical results and how they treat the object [N5-F4].

Conservation choices depend heavily on analysis because the presence of arsenic sulfide pigments has major implications for handling and treatment. The evidence states that the degradation products are highly mobile and can migrate through paint layers, varnish, and even into the support structure [N5-F4]. This means that conservation interventions such as varnish removal, sanding, or cleaning can expose friable altered paint and may actually worsen the problem by removing protective layers [N5-F4]. The evidence also warns that re-varnishing does not mitigate the problem because the mobile degradation products migrate through the varnish [N5-F4]. Therefore, analytical detection informs whether a pigment is present, how it has degraded, and what risks are associated with conservation actions [N3-F2][N5-F4]. In short, the combination of Raman and XRF is the most relevant analytical framework for distinguishing orpiment and realgar, but cross-reactivity and the photosensitivity of realgar mean interpretation must be cautious [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-F2][N5-F4].

## 6) Environmental handling and preservation strategies

The best storage and display conditions for both pigments are low light, controlled temperature, and controlled humidity. The evidence directly links light, humidity, and temperature to degradation, with light being the main trigger and humidity/temperature acting as accelerants [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-F3]. Specifically, the evidence states that the degradation of realgar and orpiment is triggered by light in the 500–670 nm range, with the highest degradation efficiency in visible light [N4-F3][N5-F4]. It also notes that high temperatures accelerate chemical reactions and overall degradation [N4-R3]. For humidity, the broader conservation context emphasizes that collections environments should monitor temperature, relative humidity, dew point, visible and UV light, and pollutants [N4-R2]. While the evidence does not provide a single recommended RH range for orpiment and realgar specifically, it clearly supports keeping relative humidity low enough to slow moisture-driven chemical reactions and avoid promoting the formation of unstable arsenic compounds [N4-R2][N4-R3].

Common conservation interventions include varnish removal, mechanical reduction of uppermost layers, and cleaning. However, the evidence warns that these interventions carry significant risks. When discolored varnishes are removed, friable altered paint can be exposed, and the altered pigment underneath may not improve in color [N5-F4]. Mechanical reduction of uppermost layers is also described as a practice used for painted furniture, but it can expose arsenic-containing species that have migrated into those layers [N5-F4]. The evidence further states that discolored and crumbling paint can be consolidated, but it cannot be readily cleaned [N5-F4]. This means that conservation choices often favor stabilization over removal when the original material is damaged and the altered layer is not easily reversible [N5-F4].

Handling affects long-term stability because arsenic-containing pigments are toxic and can release hazardous species during conservation. The evidence explicitly states that the degradation products are highly mobile and can migrate through the entire multi-layered paint system [N5-F4]. It also notes that arsenic species can collect dirt from the environment and become vulnerable to further degradation when exposed to moisture and solvents during treatment [N5-F4]. In addition, the evidence warns that conservators may not be aware that arsenic can be present in varnish layers far from the original pigment layer [N5-F4]. This handling risk is compounded by the fact that the degradation products are toxic and mobile, making them a health hazard during conservation practice [N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that orpiment can be toxic and should be handled with care [N7-R2], reinforcing that conservation handling should be protective and minimally invasive.

## 7) Integrated conclusion

In short, orpiment and realgar are both unstable arsenic sulfide pigments used in historical artworks, but they differ in their chemical formulas, degradation pathways, and conservation challenges. Orpiment is As₂S₃, while realgar is α-As₄S₄ [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R5][N1-R1][N1-R4]. Both pigments are soft, low-hardness minerals and can exist in non-stoichiometric, glassy phases [N1-R3][N1-R4][N2-F1]. Realgar degrades more complexly under light, passing through para-realgar and eventually to arsenolite, while orpiment tends to form arsenolite more directly [N2-F1][N5-F4]. Both pigments are highly sensitive to light, especially visible light in the 500–670 nm range, and both are accelerated by humidity and temperature [N4-F3][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3].

The degradation products are toxic and unstable, and they can migrate through paint layers, varnish, and even into the support structure [N5-F4]. This migration makes the pigments difficult to conserve and means that conservation interventions such as varnish removal or sanding can expose fragile altered paint without necessarily improving the appearance [N5-F4]. Analytical detection is therefore crucial: Raman microscopy and XRF are the main methods, but µRaman can produce false positives or cross-reactivity because realgar is photosensitive and can form para-realgar during analysis [N3-R4][N5-F4]. Finally, environmental handling must be conservative: low light, controlled temperature, and controlled humidity are the best preservation conditions [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-F3]. Overall, both pigments are unstable in historical artworks, but realgar’s more complex degradation pathway and orpiment’s direct formation of arsenolite make them each especially vulnerable to light-induced damage and long-term instability [N2-F1][N5-F4].

These byproducts are not only chemically unstable but also highly mobile, capable of migrating through paint layers and varnish [N5-F4].

Humidity and temperature also play a role in the degradation of arsenic sulfide pigments. The evidence in N4 states that light and humidity are key factors in the degradation of arsenic-containing pigments, and that high temperatures accelerate chemical reactions driving up the rate of overall degradation [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3]. While the direct evidence for humidity-induced degradation of orpiment and realgar is less explicit than for light, the broader conservation context clearly links environmental conditions to accelerated deterioration [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that the degradation of realgar and orpiment is triggered by light, and that the highest degradation efficiency is in visible light [N4-F3][N5-F4]. Together, these factors indicate that the degradation of both pigments is a multi-stimulus process, with light being the primary trigger and humidity/temperature acting as accelerants.

Degradation affects both color and structural integrity. Light-induced degradation causes realgar to become friable and bright yellow before progressing to a white phase, while orpiment tends to form a white arsenolite product [N5-F4]. The evidence also states that the degradation products can migrate through the entire multi-layered paint system [N5-F4], which compromises structural integrity by creating cracks, delamination, and a porous surface [N5-F4]. In addition, the physical alteration associated with chemical degradation worsens conservation problems by increasing exposure to dirt and moisture [N5-F4]. The result is irreversible damage, loss of detail and depth, and a more vulnerable object that is harder to conserve [N5-F4].

In terms of toxic byproducts, the evidence is explicit: arsenolite and arsenate compounds are formed, and arsenates can spread throughout the paint layers [N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that the presence of a medium can influence the degradation pathway, with As(V) species forming and migrating in the presence of a medium [N2-F1]. This means that historical artworks containing these pigments may have dangerous arsenic species present in unexpected locations, including varnish layers and the support structure [N5-F4]. Overall, the degradation mechanisms of orpiment and realgar are light-dominated, with humidity and temperature accelerating damage, and the byproducts are toxic, unstable, and structurally destructive [N2-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N5-F4].

In short, orpiment and realgar are both unstable arsenic sulfide pigments used in historical artworks, but they differ in their chemical formulas, degradation pathways, and conservation challenges. Orpiment is As₂S₃, while realgar is α-As₄S₄ [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R5][N1-R1][N1-R4]. Both pigments are soft, low-hardness minerals and can exist in non-stoichiometric, glassy phases [N1-R3][N1-R4][N2-F1]. Realgar degrades more complexly under light, passing through para-realgar and eventually to arsenolite, while orpiment tends to form arsenolite more directly [N2-F1][N5-F4]. Both pigments are highly sensitive to light, especially visible light in the 500–670 nm range, and both are accelerated by humidity and temperature [N4-F3][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3].

The degradation products are toxic and unstable, and they can migrate through paint layers, varnish, and even into the support structure [N5-F4]. This migration makes the pigments difficult to conserve and means that conservation interventions such as varnish removal or sanding can expose fragile altered paint without necessarily improving the appearance [N5-F4]. Analytical detection is therefore crucial: Raman microscopy and XRF are the main methods, but µRaman can produce false positives or cross-reactivity because realgar is photosensitive and can form para-realgar during analysis [N3-R4][N5-F4]. Finally, environmental handling must be conservative: low light, controlled temperature, and controlled humidity are the best preservation conditions [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-F3]. Overall, both pigments are unstable in historical artworks, but realgar’s more complex degradation pathway and orpiment’s direct formation of arsenolite make them each especially vulnerable to light-induced damage and long-term instability [N2-F1][N5-F4].
